title: Workflow Quality and Maintainability
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of workflow quality and maintainability and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to workflow quality and maintainability.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on workflow quality and maintainability. Maintainable workflow design uses clear names, small jobs, tested shared logic, reviewed permission changes, and documentation that explains ownership and recovery. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Workflow Quality and Maintainability matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Maintainable workflow design uses clear names, small jobs, tested shared logic, reviewed permission changes, and documentation that explains ownership and recovery. Migrations and maintenance should preserve observable behavior while removing legacy assumptions. Inventory triggers, permissions, dependencies, runner assumptions, and rollback needs before changing workflows.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Maintainable workflow design uses clear names, small jobs, tested shared logic, reviewed permission changes, and documentation that explains ownership and recovery. Migrations and maintenance should preserve observable behavior while removing legacy assumptions. Inventory triggers, permissions, dependencies, runner assumptions, and rollback needs before changing workflows. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Consistent naming conventions
items.text: For consistent naming conventions, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Small, focused workflows
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Clear job boundaries
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Minimal permissions
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

items.title: Documented inputs and outputs
items.text: Write one step output as `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, then declare job outputs if a downstream job needs the value. Use `$GITHUB_ENV` for values needed by later steps in the same job.

content_blocks.code:
name: Controlled workflow review
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Review permissions, triggers, artifacts, and recovery evidence"
content_blocks.expected_output: The manually started job prints a checklist reminder; a real review must validate the actual workflow and retain reviewed evidence.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to workflow quality and maintainability. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain workflow quality and maintainability, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Recognize common failure patterns, migrate safely, and keep knowledge current as platform behavior evolves.

content.task: Apply workflow quality and maintainability to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Maintainable workflow design uses clear names, small jobs, tested shared logic, reviewed permission changes, and documentation that explains ownership and recovery.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Maintainable workflow design uses clear names, small jobs, tested shared logic, reviewed permission changes, and documentation that explains ownership and recovery. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Maintainable workflow design uses clear names, small jobs, tested shared logic, reviewed permission changes, and documentation that explains ownership and recovery.

Migrations and maintenance should preserve observable behavior while removing legacy assumptions. Inventory triggers, permissions, dependencies, runner assumptions, and rollback needs before changing workflows.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
